title: Should You Pay Off Your Car Loan or Credit Card First?
description: Car loan or credit card first? In most cases the card wins because its rate is higher. See the math, the exceptions, and how to plan the payoff order.

paa.question: Should I pay off my car loan or credit card first?
paa.answer: Usually the credit card. Card rates often run 20% or more, while many car loans charge under 10%, so each extra dollar on the card saves more interest. Keep paying at least the minimum on both, and keep the car loan current first, since missing it can put the car at risk.

bodyHtml:
If you have a car loan and a credit card balance and some extra money each month, the order you pay them off changes how much interest you pay and how soon you are debt free. For most people the answer is the credit card first. Here is why, when the answer flips, and how to see the difference in dollars.

Why the Credit Card Usually Comes First

Interest is charged on the balance at the account's rate, so the debt with the highest rate costs the most per dollar owed. Credit cards commonly charge 20% to 29% APR. Many car loans charge somewhere between 5% and 10%.

One thousand dollars on a card at 24% costs about $240 a year in interest. The same $1,000 on a car loan at 7% costs about $70. An extra payment on the card therefore saves more than three times as much. Paying the highest-rate debt first is called the avalanche method, and it gives the lowest total interest.

A Worked Example

Say you owe $4,000 on a card at 24% with a $150 minimum, and $15,000 on a car loan at 7% with a payment of about $297. You can put an extra $200 a month toward debt.

If the extra $200 goes to the card first, the card is gone in about 14 months. Its freed-up payment then rolls onto the car loan. Both debts are paid off in about 34 months, with about $2,391 in total interest.

If the extra $200 goes to the car loan first, the card sits at its minimum and keeps charging 24%. Both debts are paid off in about 35 months, with about $3,291 in total interest.

Same income, same total payment each month. Choosing the card first saves about $900 and finishes a month sooner. These figures assume fixed rates and no new card spending.

When the Car Loan Should Come First

  • You are behind on the car loan. A missed car payment can lead to late fees and, eventually, repossession. Get it current before sending extra anywhere else.
  • Your card is at 0% for a promotional period. Until the promotion ends, the car loan may be the higher rate. Plan to clear the card before the rate jumps.
  • You need to sell or trade the car soon and owe more than it is worth. Paying down the loan can close that gap.
  • Your car loan has an unusually high rate, above your card's. Then the avalanche method points at the car.

Do Not Skip the Minimums

Whichever debt gets the extra money, the other still needs its minimum every month. Missing a minimum adds fees, can raise the card's rate, and hurts your credit score, which costs more than the order ever saves.

It also helps to stop adding to the card while you pay it down. New charges at 24% undo the plan faster than any extra payment can keep up. Our guides on paying off credit card debt faster and whether to pay off a car loan early go deeper on each side.

Plan the Order With Real Dates

The order is easier to stick to when you can see the finish line. Write down each debt, its rate, its balance and its minimum, then decide where the extra goes and how much it is.

Forgenta does this for you: it looks at your income, bills and debts, recommends which debt to pay first, and shows the date each one is paid off and the interest the plan saves, so the order is a decision you can check rather than a guess.

What About the Snowball Method?

Some people prefer the snowball method instead: pay the smallest balance first, whatever its rate, then roll that payment into the next one. It costs more in interest than the avalanche method, but the quick early win keeps some people motivated.

With a car loan and one credit card, the two methods often agree, because the card is usually both the smaller balance and the higher rate. They disagree when the card balance is large and the car loan is nearly paid off. In that case the snowball says finish the car loan first, and the avalanche says keep going on the card.

If you are choosing between them, look at the dollar difference. When it is small, pick the one you will actually stick with. When it is large, as in the worked example above, the avalanche is usually worth the patience.

Whichever you choose, write the order down and keep it. Switching targets every few months is the most expensive plan of all, because each debt keeps charging its full rate while the extra money moves around.

Once the card is gone, keep it from coming back. Leave the card open if it has no annual fee, since closing it can raise your utilization, but take it out of your wallet or phone until the car loan is paid off too. The habit that cleared the balance is the same habit that keeps it at zero.

The Bottom Line

In most cases, pay the credit card first and the car loan second, because the card's higher rate makes every extra dollar there worth more. Keep both minimums paid, keep the car loan current, and watch for the exceptions above. The right order can save hundreds of dollars without changing what you pay each month.

faqs.q: Is it better to pay off a car loan early?
faqs.a: Only after higher-rate debt such as credit cards is gone and you have an emergency fund. A low-rate car loan is one of the cheaper debts to carry.

faqs.q: Does paying off a credit card help my credit score more than a car loan?
faqs.a: Usually yes, because lower card balances reduce your credit utilization, which weighs heavily in most scores.
Paying minimums on every debt and sending all extra money to the highest-rate debt first, then rolling that payment to the next one.
